subject: english-language
title: Cameron and the Myth of Mars and Venus
welcome_lead: Deborah Cameron tears up the self-help shelf. Her meta-analyses argue the gender gap in talk is largely a marketing myth.
meta_desc: Deborah Cameron's critique of difference and the myth of gendered talk at A-Level English Language.
final_note: You have read Cameron's case for caution — small effects, big stereotypes, and a publishing industry happy to amplify them.

concepts.def: Cameron (2007) — the popular belief that men and women speak differently, used to sell self-help.
Reviews of many studies (Hyde 2005, Cameron 2007) find very small average gender differences in language behaviour.
Mehl et al. (2007) found women and men used roughly 16,000 words a day — no significant difference.
Awareness of stereotypes can shape behaviour, creating a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Variation within men or within women dwarfs average differences between them.
Popular gender-difference books succeed because they confirm pre-existing beliefs.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Cameron surveyed psychological and sociolinguistic literature to ask: are men and women linguistically different in measurable, meaningful ways?

Conclusion: average differences are tiny; within-group variation is vast; popular books overclaim.

Matthias Mehl's team recorded speakers' actual word counts and found women and men averaged near-identical totals — around 16,000 a day.

The 'women talk three times more than men' factoid had no empirical basis.

When speakers are reminded of gender stereotypes they may behave in line with them. Difference becomes self-reinforcing.

Cameron's argument: studies that find difference must control for context, status and stereotype activation.
